mountain range noun

also mountain chain, unbroken chain, range of mountains, chain of mountains

modern

Traupman 205: mountain chain

montēs perpetuī

noun phrase: montēs, montium m. pl., with perpetuus, unbroken

a mountain chain, a mountain range

Traupman’s phrase: mountains that run on without a break. Perpetuus is Pliny’s word for the unbroken ridges of the Apennines (below).

Other words

  • jugum, jugī n. — a ridge; a chain of mountains

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Lewis & Short: “a height or summit of a mountain, a ridge; also, a chain of mountains” (Verg. E. 5.76; Caes. BC 1.70); M-O s.v. mountain range or chain; Traupman 202: Alpium juga, the Alpine chain

    First a yoke; of mountains, the ridge, and so a range (see ridge). Morgan–Owens gives it for a mountain range, from the naturalists Desfontaines and Pallas.

  • perpetuīs jugīs tendere — to stretch in an unbroken range

    also used · classical · Plin. NH 3.48: Apennīnus perpetuīs jugīs ab Alpibus tendēns ad Siculum fretum (Lewis & Short s.v. perpetuus); Traupman 201, 203

    The verb phrase, for saying where a range runs: Pliny’s words, which Traupman borrows.

Examples

  • nam Osoitsa ad rādīcēs Haemī jacet, quī perpetuīs jugīs per tōtam Bulgariam ad Pontum ūsque tendit

    for Osoitsa lies at the foot of the Haemus, which stretches in an unbroken range across all Bulgaria to the Black Seacomposed

  • Appennīnus mōns perpetuīs jugīs ab Alpibus tendēns ad …

    the Apennines extending in an unbroken chain from the Alps to …Traupman 203

See also mountain, ridge.

SourcesLewis & Short: jugum · Lewis & Short: perpetuus

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 201–203, 205.

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. mountain range or chain.
